lead: Today's readings are about what we carry and what we forget. In the Epistle Paul, an old man in prison, pleads for Onesimus, a runaway slave who has become his son in the faith, and promises to repay whatever Onesimus owes. In the Gospel the disciples cross the lake having forgotten to bring bread, and Jesus uses their worry about bread to warn them of another kind of yeast, the wrong teaching that can spread through a whole community. The key words are welcome and remember.

r.h: Welcome him as you would welcome me
set: Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters and the only one addressed chiefly to a single person on a private matter. Paul writes from prison (vv. 1, 9, 13) to Philemon, a Christian of Colossae in whose house the church met (v. 2; compare Colossians 4:9). Philemon's slave Onesimus had left him, perhaps with some debt or loss to his master, and had met Paul, who brought him to faith (v. 10). Where Paul was in prison is not certain: Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have each been proposed.

Paul now sends Onesimus back, with this letter in his hand. He does not give an order. He asks as a friend, an “old man” (v. 9) and the one who brought Philemon himself to Christ (v. 19). Our verses are the heart of the request.
str: v. 17: “welcome him as you would welcome me.”
vv. 18–19: if Onesimus owes anything, Paul will repay it.
vv. 21–22: Paul trusts Philemon to do even more, and hopes to visit.
kw: The word means one who shares in something with another; it is of the same family as koinōnia, “communion”. Paul reminds Philemon that they share a common life in Christ, and that this is stronger than the law about a runaway slave.
A word from the business of the time, used for putting a debt on someone's account. Paul takes Onesimus's debt on himself, as Christ took on himself the debt of us all.
The Greek word splanchna means the inward parts, the seat of strong feeling. Paul asks Philemon to bring peace to his deepest affection, by receiving Onesimus well.
vv: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
Paul does not say “forgive him” or “spare him”. He says: receive him as you would receive me. Onesimus takes Paul's place at Philemon's door.
If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.
Paul does not pretend there is no wrong. He admits that Onesimus may owe something, and then pays for it himself. This is love that deals honestly with the loss.
I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it.
Paul takes the pen from the secretary and writes these words himself, like a signature on a promissory note. Having said this, he gently remembers that Philemon owes him his very self.
ch: The Church reads this letter as a small page of the Gospel: in Christ a slave becomes “a beloved brother” (v. 16). Paul does not here condemn the institution of slavery in so many words, but by teaching that a slave is a brother he plants the seed that later grew. The Church today teaches that slavery and the trade in human beings are a grave offence against human dignity (CCC 2414; Gaudium et Spes 27). The Fathers also saw in Paul's offer a picture of Christ: as Paul stands between Onesimus and his master, so Christ stands between us and the Father and takes our debt upon himself. An old tradition identifies Onesimus with the bishop of Ephesus of that name, but this is not certain.

set: The scene follows two controversies. The Pharisees and Sadducees have asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, and he has refused them and left (16:1–4). He and his disciples cross the Sea of Galilee to the other side, and the disciples discover they have no bread. Jesus then speaks to them of yeast.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were different groups, often in disagreement with each other. Matthew names them together to show that the teaching Jesus warns against is not one party's alone: it is any teaching that closes the heart to the signs God gives. The Pharisees were pious and respected, and Jesus often agrees with them (Matthew 23:2–3). The warning is about a spirit of testing God and demanding signs, which can arise anywhere.
str: v. 5: the disciples have forgotten bread.
v. 6: Jesus warns: beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
v. 7: the disciples think he is speaking of bread.
vv. 8–11: Jesus reproaches their little faith; he recalls the two feedings.
v. 12: they understand: the yeast is teaching.
kw: Yeast is a little thing that works silently until all the dough is changed. In the Bible it can mean good influence (Matthew 13:33) or bad (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here it is the bad: a teaching that spreads quietly.
Matthew uses this word of the disciples several times (6:30; 8:26; 14:31). It is not unbelief but weak, anxious trust. Jesus does not drive them away; he teaches them.

Matthew uses a different word for the baskets of the first feeding (14:20, kophinoi) and for the second (15:37, spyrides). The Gospel keeps the memory of what the disciples gathered, as proof that Jesus always gives more than enough.
vv: You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread?
The disciples have just seen Jesus feed thousands twice from a few loaves. To worry about a lack of bread in his company is to forget who is with them.
Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
Jesus calls them to remember. Faith in the Gospel is partly memory: remembering what the Lord has done and trusting that he will do it again.
he had not told them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
Matthew gives the answer to the riddle himself. “Teaching” (didachē) is the way of thinking passed from teacher to disciple. Yeast of bread feeds the body; false teaching can spoil the soul.
ch: The Church has always read the two feedings as signs of the Eucharist (CCC 1335): Jesus gives bread that does not run out. The Fathers also took the warning about yeast as a call to guard the purity of faith and of teaching. For this the Church holds the Apostles' teaching in her creeds and teaches that the faithful must recognize true teaching from false (CCC 85–88). Yet yeast is not evil in itself; Jesus says the Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast hidden in flour (Matthew 13:33). The yeast of the Gospel, quiet and strong, is what the Church is called to be in the world.

qa: Did Paul accept slavery, since he sends Onesimus back?

Paul never calls slavery good. In the world of his day it was part of the whole order of society, and he does not here attack it directly. But he speaks of Onesimus as “my child” (v. 10) and “a beloved brother” (v. 16), and he asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul himself. When a slave is a brother, the old order is already undone from within. The Church teaches today that slavery is a grave evil that offends the dignity of the human person (CCC 2414).
study: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “as you would welcome me”. Whom is the Lord asking me to welcome in this way?
Jesus says, “Do you not remember?” What has the Lord done for me that I must remember when I am anxious about tomorrow?
